subject: Civil Engineering
title: Seepage and Internal Erosion
description: A short lesson to help you apply Seepage and Internal Erosion.

hook.text: Water always finds a way through — or under — a dam. Uncontrolled seepage destroys it.

buildup.text: Seepage creates hydraulic gradients — water pressure drives flow through tiny pores.

discovery.text: If the gradient is too steep, water carries soil particles away — this is piping, and it's deadly.

twist.text: A small leak grows into a tunnel through the dam — progressive erosion leads to catastrophic breach.

climax.text: Filters — layers of graded sand and gravel — catch particles while letting water pass safely.

punchline.text: A dam doesn't fail from the water over it — it fails from the water through it.

quiz.question: What is piping in the context of dam safety?
options: Installing pipes through the dam to release excess water
Internal erosion where seeping water carries soil particles away, creating a tunnel through the dam
The process of pumping water from the reservoir for irrigation

details.summary: Seepage is the movement of water through and beneath a dam, driven by the difference in water level between the reservoir and downstream. Internal erosion occurs when seepage forces carry soil particles out of the dam body or foundation.
details.whyItMatters: Internal erosion is the most common cause of embankment dam failure. It occurs invisibly inside the dam, often with little warning before sudden and catastrophic breach.
takeaways: All dams experience some seepage, which must be controlled not eliminated
Internal erosion removes soil particles progressively, enlarging seepage channels
Filters and drains prevent particle migration while allowing water to pass safely

faq.question: What is piping failure in an embankment dam?
faq.answer: Piping begins when seepage velocities become high enough to detach and carry soil particles from the dam core or foundation. The removed particles enlarge the seepage path, increasing flow and erosion rate in a self-reinforcing cycle.

faq.question: How do filters prevent internal erosion in dams?
faq.answer: Filters are layers of carefully graded granular material placed against the dam core. The filter particles are sized small enough to prevent core particles from passing through, yet large enough to allow water to drain freely.
